title: NVIDIA Run:ai Is Now Open Source as Part of NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA open-sources the entire Run:ai GPU and AI workload orchestration platform (KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management, Workload Map) as part of DSX AI Factory, with eight neocloud and infra partners integrating it. It also highlights Model Streamer and Grove as companion open source tools for cutting inference cold-start time and orchestrating multicomponent serving.

insights.claim: NVIDIA is releasing the full Run:ai GPU and AI workload orchestration platform as open source and positioning it as the open foundation of its DSX AI Factory Platform, rather than keeping it a paid proprietary product.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Commoditizing the orchestration layer deepens the NVIDIA software moat around its GPUs and lowers adoption friction for neoclouds and enterprises.
insights.quote: Today, NVIDIA is making the full NVIDIA Run:ai platform available as open source software

insights.claim: The open source Run:ai Community Product on NGC requires no paid Run:ai subscription or NVIDIA support entitlement, but NVIDIA enterprise support is not included, so support remains the monetizable tier via Mission Control, AI Enterprise and marketplaces.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Open core with paid support suggests NVIDIA monetizes via enterprise bundles and hardware pull-through, not orchestration licences.
insights.quote: No paid NVIDIA Run:ai subscription or NVIDIA support entitlement is required for the Community Product
insights.locator: How to adopt open source NVIDIA Run:ai

insights.claim: The release is modular: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management and Workload Map can each be adopted independently, letting teams with an existing platform fill specific gaps without taking the whole stack.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Modular components lower the barrier for piecemeal adoption, which spreads NVIDIA-originated primitives into third-party stacks.
insights.locator: This post details the open source release

insights.claim: Eight DSX ecosystem partners (Crusoe, Mirantis, Nebius, OpenNebula Systems, Rafay, Saturn Cloud, Spectro Cloud, vCluster) are integrating open source Run:ai into their offerings, spanning managed Kubernetes, one-click cloud apps, and white-label inference.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Shows which neoclouds and infra software vendors are aligning with NVIDIA's software stack; a read on neocloud differentiation moving up the stack.
insights.locator: Adopt through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners

insights.claim: Saturn Cloud is using Run:ai to let AI cloud operators launch white-label inference services with per-token metering and automated billing, indicating GPU clouds are moving toward token-priced inference products built on shared orchestration.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Token-metered inference on top of commodity orchestration suggests neocloud margins hinge on utilization and billing, not on the scheduler.

insights.claim: Open source Run:ai gives partners direct access to orchestration code so they can ship their own DSX AI factory solutions faster and respond to customer requirements, making NVIDIA's software a shared substrate that partners differentiate on top of.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Shared open substrate reduces rivals' incentive to build competing orchestration, reinforcing NVIDIA-centric ecosystem lock-in.
insights.locator: Open source NVIDIA Run:ai gives NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners

insights.claim: KAI Scheduler was released under Apache 2.0 and contributed to CNCF as a Sandbox project, with all scheduler development happening in the community repository, which is the upstream engine of Run:ai.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Neutral CNCF governance makes it easier for competing cloud vendors to adopt an NVIDIA-originated scheduler.

insights.claim: KAI Scheduler targets GPU utilization via gang scheduling (all-or-nothing placement of multipod jobs), fair-share and quota allocation, topology awareness, bin-packing, GPU sharing (MIG, MPS, time sharing, HaMi) and DRA support.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Utilization of installed GPUs is a key lever on AI infrastructure ROI; software that raises it reduces demand for incremental capacity per workload.
insights.locator: KAI Scheduler is purpose-built for GPU workloads at scale

insights.claim: Run:ai's proprietary fractional GPU implementation has been retired in favor of CUDA 13.4-native fractioning, where the driver enforces a hard memory limit per workload, and the new open source operator is the Kubernetes layer for consuming it.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Pushing GPU sharing into CUDA itself makes multi-tenant GPU slicing a platform-native feature, strengthening CUDA lock-in.
insights.quote: the proprietary implementation has been retired in favor of the native capability available in CUDA 13.4
insights.locator: GPU Fractioning: An operator for GPU fractions

insights.claim: Fractional GPUs are aimed at workloads that do not need a GPU's full memory, such as interactive notebooks and smaller-model inference, and the author calls this one of the most widely used Run:ai capabilities among ML teams.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: A large share of real GPU demand is underutilizing small workloads, so sharing can absorb demand without new hardware.

insights.claim: KAI Resource Management lets platform teams guarantee shares of a heterogeneous cluster by team and department, for example reserving 50% of capacity for research while preventing any one team from monopolizing the rest, replacing spreadsheet-tracked quotas.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Organizational quota governance is a gating feature for enterprise shared-GPU clusters, relevant to internal chargeback and utilization.
insights.locator: KAI Resource Management: The organizational layer

insights.claim: Workload Map defines each Kubernetes AI workload type (PyTorchJob, RayCluster, JobSet, KServe InferenceService, Dynamo graph deployment) once, so schedulers and tools need not hardcode each CRD; it is deliberately narrow and does not schedule, queue, autoscale or span clusters.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Standardizing workload descriptions is an attempt to own the interface between Kubernetes and AI tooling, a layer many vendors compete for.

insights.claim: Cold-starting an inference workload on Kubernetes can take several minutes during which GPUs are allocated but idle while model weights load; Model Streamer reads weights concurrently and streams them straight into GPU memory.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Idle allocated GPUs during model loading are a hidden cost of autoscaled inference; faster loading raises effective utilization.

insights.claim: Model Streamer is integrated upstream in vLLM and SGLang and documented by AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure; Azure benchmarks on eight H100 VMs show 3x-6x faster loading and a steady 80 Gbps versus roughly 40 Gbps for the default path.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler endorsement shows an NVIDIA-originated open tool becoming de facto inference infrastructure across rival clouds.
insights.locator: Microsoft Azure: Azure Blob Storage integration

insights.claim: Storage vendors report Model Streamer loads into GPU memory from shared storage faster than local NVMe: WEKA 3.5 seconds (about 40% faster), VAST Data 1.7 seconds (60% improvement), and DDN streamed the 65.5 GB Qwen3-32B across 8 GPUs in under four seconds, saving up to 10% of daily GPU runtime.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Shared high-performance storage can beat local NVMe for weight loading, supporting the case for AI data platform vendors; figures are vendor-reported.

insights.claim: Agentic pipelines, disaggregated serving and mixture-of-experts training consist of multiple connected components that must scale together, and Grove provides a Kubernetes API for them with topology-aware autoscaling and hierarchical gang scheduling so prefill and decode start as all-or-nothing units.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Workload shapes are shifting from single pods to coupled graphs, raising the importance of orchestration software for inference economics.
insights.locator: Grove: One API, any inference architecture

insights.claim: On GB200 NVL72, Grove automatically manages ComputeDomain resources, enabling multinode NVLink performance through a single annotation instead of hand-authored YAML, and it supports llm-d and Volcano as scheduler backends with Kueue in progress.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Software that makes rack-scale NVLink systems easy to use lowers operational barriers to GB200 deployment.
